title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Stone and terrazzo restoration
audience: Solo operators and team owners in any service business who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the floors you restore well, the room sizes you can price at a sustainable rate, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. Terrazzo and stone restoration is usually a one-off job per building or floor, so repeat need is weaker than for a maintenance service. Say that in your criteria, and decide how you will fill the calendar between projects. Write one short profile for each segment on your list, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market (business.gov.au, 24 September 2024). These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat or project need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. The research did not verify a prospect channel for terrazzo. Property managers, builders and trade referrals were searched, and no verified evidence was found, so any of them is a hypothesis to test rather than a list you can rely on. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Use only business contact details published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. For stone and terrazzo, a planning or building permit can show a refurbishment at application or approval stage. In Victoria, some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register in the Victorian open data portal (DataVic, updated 5 November 2026). Check your own council's register. A permit shows that a project is happening, not who will restore its floors, so treat it as a reason to qualify, not as a prospect list. Victoria also publishes building permit activity by suburb or postcode, which helps you choose areas to market in, but it does not confirm owner or builder names (Data Vic, 28 August 2026). Do not turn address data into individual contact.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the project. It makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or from a published notice, such as a planning application for a refurbishment in the same street. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026), so a specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage. Once a prospect replies, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline before you quote, as Business Queensland advises (Business Queensland, 16 November 2022; Queensland guidance).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced replies that became paid work. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the floor types, room sizes, area and repeat-need criteria for the stone work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as a council planning register, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence and insurance rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A restorer covers three suburbs in Victoria. A planning application for refurbishment works is listed on the council's register for a multi-storey building in one of them. The building's general enquiries address is published on its website.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the restorer send a sales message to the building's manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The restorer does not send a sales email just because the address is published. The Spam Act covers business addresses, and publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the restorer first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the restorer waits for an invitation or uses a route the manager has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the restorer checks the register before calling. Any message that does go out names the planning application, says how the business learned of it, makes one specific point about the floors in the application, offers one small next step and asks one question. The restorer does not contact individual owners or tenants using private details, and does not enter the building without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, floor type, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop. Gap: no verified referral channel exists for terrazzo.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the stone work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Use planning registers as reasons to qualify, and never use private information to make contact.
Gap: no verified property-manager, builder or referral channel exists for terrazzo. Test each prospect type before relying on it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A building manager with a project inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A council register shows a planning application for works at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details
Go into the common area to look at the floors before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not name the Spam Act 2003 or cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing (OAIC)
officialReferences.pageDate: page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019
officialReferences.covers: Says the direct-marketing rules apply to personal information that is publicly available, with no general exemption for public information. Applies only where the Privacy Act covers the business. Publisher: OAIC.
